performers: Geraldine Farrar, soprano; orchestra conducted by Walter B. Rogers
intro: In the Habanera from Act I of Carmen, Carmen sings that love obeys no law, over a bass that repeats the same dance step. Geraldine Farrar sings both verses in French in this acoustic recording made in 1914.

sections.label: A · Chromatic verse over habanera bass
A′ · Second verse, descending theme returns
sections.mNote: The descending tune returns for the second verse.

sections.label: B′ · Refrain and closing warning
sections.mNote: The major-key refrain returns, with an extended close.

cues.title: Habanera, Carmen’s entrance
cues.text: The bass repeats the habanera rhythm throughout: a dotted quaver, a semiquaver, then two quavers. Above it the voice descends by semitones. Carmen enters with a song about a bird that nobody can tame.
cues.evidence: Bizet’s own piano reduction, Choudens vocal score (archive.org copy catalogued 1883), no. 5, pp. 49–50: the repeated bass and chromatic vocal line. https://archive.org/details/carmenopracomi00bize
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Refrain in D major
cues.text: At the refrain, “L’amour est enfant de Bohème”, the music moves from D minor to D major and the bass keeps its dance rhythm. The words warn that anyone Carmen loves should beware.
cues.evidence: Choudens vocal score (copy catalogued 1883), no. 5, pp. 51–52: the major-key refrain beginning “L’amour est enfant de Bohème”. The verse-and-refrain design is also described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habanera_(aria).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Borrowing from Iradier
cues.text: Bizet built Carmen’s entrance from Sebastián Iradier’s song El arreglito and wrote the Habanera’s words himself. Choudens’s vocal score acknowledged the Spanish source in a footnote beneath the opening bars.
cues.evidence: Hugh Macdonald, Bizet Catalogue, Carmen: borrowing from Iradier and attribution of the Habanera text to Bizet. The Choudens vocal score, p. 49, prints the footnote “Imitée d’une chanson espagnole. Propriété des Éditeurs du Ménestrel.” https://hdwlabs.artsci.wustl.edu/bizet/works/Carmen.html https://archive.org/details/carmenopracomi00bize

cues.title: Closing refrain
cues.text: The refrain returns, and the words about love now address “you” directly. The repeating bass continues under both verses, and Carmen stretches the phrase above it while the dance rhythm holds.
cues.evidence: Choudens vocal score (copy catalogued 1883), no. 5, pp. 57–59, closing refrain. Bru Zane’s Carmen study discusses Bizet’s pointed use of the singular “tu”: https://www.bruzanemediabase.com/exploration/oeuvres/carmen-meilhac-l-halevy-bizet
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

fields.value: French-language solo recording of the Habanera, with orchestral accompaniment; both verses and the closing refrain
fields.note: A complete commercial aria side, not a recording of the surrounding stage scene. The English title on the disc describes the aria; the performance is in French. Ensemble participation in the stage score is not claimed for this solo recording.

fields.value: Four stylus transfers were made; the selected friendly-filename transfer was preferred by the digitising engineer. Flat and equalised versions are described, with 500 Hz turnover for the latter.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public domain: Bizet’s 1875 score and the nineteenth-century French text
fields.note: Bizet died in 1875; the Habanera’s text is his own. This is the original French aria, not a modern translation or arrangement.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Public domain in the United States: commercially published in 1915, before the 1923 statutory boundary
fields.note: The Talking Machine World, January 1915, p. 62, lists Victor 87210 under ‘The February Red Seal Records’. This establishes publication independently of the December 1914 session and the Archive’s generic 1914 date. Under the Classics Protection and Access Act, protection for pre-1923 publications ended on 31 December 2021. No worldwide-rights claim is made.

composer.epithet: Composer of an opera in which a factory worker sings that love obeys no law, while four bass notes beneath her voice keep the dance going.
facts: Paris Conservatoire; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Fromental Halévy
Prix de Rome 1857 · Les Pêcheurs de perles 1863 · Carmen 1875
Jeux d’enfants for piano duet · L’Arlésienne for the spoken theatre
composer.background:
Outside the bullring, Carmen tells José that she will not return to him. Inside, the spectators cheer Escamillo. Bizet keeps both scenes audible: the tune of the Toreador Song is heard from inside the arena while José pleads with Carmen and then kills her. The melody first appeared in the opera as Escamillo’s song to the crowd. Carmen opened at the Paris Opéra-Comique on 3 March 1875. Three months later its composer was dead, aged thirty-six. He had spent most of his working life trying to get an opera to stay on the stage.

Georges Bizet was born in Paris on 25 October 1838. His father Adolphe taught singing; his mother Aimée played the piano, and her brother François Delsarte was a singing teacher. Bizet entered the Conservatoire in October 1848, before his tenth birthday. Antoine Marmontel taught him piano, François Benoist organ, and Fromental Halévy composition. He won prizes for piano, fugue and organ. Charles Gounod was an especially important example to him, as a composer who made a career in the theatre without giving up the suppleness of a sung phrase.
